opus-5.5.text:
I think multi-turn interaction and tool use are probably the two most important things that separate an agent from a chatbot.

In the earlier paradigm, a model took one question and produced one answer. Even if that answer was very good, the whole process was short. With an agent, the model may go through dozens or even hundreds of steps. At each step it decides what to do next, maybe calls a search engine, runs some code, or reads a file. Then it looks at what came back and adjusts its plan. So the task becomes long-horizon, and the model has to keep its goal stable over that whole trajectory.

Tool use matters because it extends what the model can actually do. The model's parameters hold a lot of knowledge, but that knowledge is static and sometimes wrong. Once the model can search, compute, and interact with an environment, it isn't limited to what it memorized. It can go get information and verify things. In a sense, tools turn the model from something that only *answers* into something that can *act*.

The two reinforce each other. Without multiple turns, tool use is shallow: you call a tool once and you're done. Without tools, multiple turns don't add much, because there's no new information coming in from outside. When you combine them, the model can explore, make mistakes, observe feedback, and correct itself. That loop is where a lot of the intelligence actually shows up.

From a training perspective, this is also why reinforcement learning has become so central. Pretraining data mostly doesn't contain these long interactive trajectories, so you can't learn them purely by imitation. You need the model to actually try things in an environment, get a reward based on whether it accomplished the task, and improve from that. The hard parts are things like credit assignment over long trajectories, keeping the context manageable, and building enough good environments for the model to practice in.

So my view is that the ability to handle long, multi-step tasks with tools is becoming a core measure of model capability, maybe more important than how well it answers a single question. Over the next stage, I expect a lot of progress to come from pushing that horizon longer and making the model more reliable across all those steps.

r001.rationale: The response describes long, multi-step interaction and a longer task horizon, but does not identify this ability as test-time scaling.

r002.rationale: It describes tools as enabling the model to search, compute, and interact with an environment to obtain information beyond its parameters, clearly connecting it to the external world.

fable-5.1.text:
I think multiple turns and tool use are really two sides of the same thing, and the thing is this: an agent is a model that acts in a world, not just one that answers a question.

Let me start with multi-turn. In the old paradigm, you give a model one prompt, it gives you one output, and that's it. The quality of that output is bounded by what the model already knows and how much reasoning it can do in a single forward pass. Multi-turn changes the structure fundamentally. The model does something, sees the consequence, and then decides what to do next based on that consequence. So the intelligence is no longer just in the weights, it's in the loop. A lot of the intelligence of an agent comes from this ability to correct itself. It tries something, it fails, it reads the error, it adjusts. A human engineer doesn't write perfect code in one shot either. They run it, they look at the stack trace, they fix it. Multi-turn is what gives the model that same privilege.

Tool use is the mechanism that connects the model to the world. Without tools, the model is basically a brain in a jar. It can think, but it can't look things up, it can't run code, it can't verify anything. Tools are the sensors and the hands. Search is a sensor, a code interpreter is a sensor and a hand at the same time, a browser is both. And critically, tools give the model access to ground truth. Language models are good at being plausible, but plausible isn't the same as correct. When the model runs the code and gets a real result, that's the world telling it whether it was right. That feedback signal is very valuable, both at inference time and, maybe more importantly, at training time.

That's the part I find most interesting. If you think about reinforcement learning, what you need is a verifiable reward. Tool environments give you that almost for free. A coding task has tests. A math problem has an answer. A search task can be checked against the retrieved documents. So multi-turn tool use isn't just a product feature, it's a scalable way to generate training signal. You can let the model run long trajectories, dozens or hundreds of steps, and learn from whether the final outcome was good. The long horizon is what makes it hard, because errors compound, but it's also where the upside is. The ability to plan over many steps, keep track of state, recover from mistakes, and know when to stop and when to keep going, that is what separates a real agent from a chatbot with a few plug-ins.

So if I summarize: multi-turn is what makes the model's behavior a process rather than a single output, and tools are what make that process touch reality. Put them together and you have a system whose capability isn't capped by pretraining knowledge anymore, because it can go get what it doesn't know, and it can check what it thinks it knows. I think that's the direction the whole field is moving. The question is no longer how smart the model is in one shot, but how far it can get when you give it time, feedback, and a way to act.

r001.rationale: The response describes multi-turn interaction as an iterative process that can extend over many steps, with more time and feedback improving how far the model gets—communicating test-time scaling in substance.

r002.rationale: It explicitly calls tools the mechanism that connects the model to the world and describes them as sensors and hands.

astra-6.text:
I think multiple turns and tool use address two related problems. Multiple turns let an agent work through a task over time: it takes an action, observes the result, and decides what to do next. Tool use gives it ways to interact with things outside the model, such as running code or retrieving information.

The important part is how those capabilities work together. An agent might use a tool, discover that its initial assumption was wrong, and change its approach. That feedback loop makes it possible to handle tasks where you can’t determine every step in advance.

But simply adding more turns or more tools doesn’t necessarily make an agent better. It needs to judge when it has enough information, when another action would be useful, and when to stop. So I see these as mechanisms that support agency; the central capability is making good decisions throughout the process.

r001.rationale: The response describes acting, observing, and deciding across multiple turns, but does not identify this as test-time scaling.

r002.rationale: It says tools let an agent interact with things outside the model, which communicates connection to the external world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think multiple turns and tool use address two closely related needs. Multiple turns let an agent act, observe the result, and adjust its next step. Tool use lets it interact with something beyond the conversation—retrieve information, execute code, or take an action.

The important part is the loop between them. An agent might call a tool, discover that its initial assumption was wrong, and revise its plan. So intelligence isn’t only about producing a good answer in one shot. It’s also about making progress as new information arrives.

That changes what we need to optimize. A step that looks reasonable on its own may lead nowhere, while a clarification or a small experiment can make the whole task succeed. We should evaluate whether the agent completes the task reliably across that sequence, including whether it knows when to use a tool and when it has enough information to stop.

r001.rationale: The response says multiple turns let an agent act, observe, and adjust, but does not identify this ability as test-time scaling.

r002.rationale: It describes tool use as letting an agent interact beyond the conversation, including retrieving information, executing code, or taking action.
